interactions.summary: A student answers that Jephthah's daughter is the hero because she understands the vow and still offers herself, and Jiang agrees, elevating her all the way to paradise despite the normal Christian rule against non-Christians entering heaven.

Jiang retells the biblical scene: Jephthah vows a sacrifice for victory, his daughter walks in first, and she voluntarily offers herself so her father can keep the vow without bearing the direct guilt of murdering her; Jiang reads this as a selfless act of love that earns paradise.

A student asks whether simple willingness to die is what gets one into paradise, Jiang rejects that reduction and says the elevating thing is the selfless act of love itself, then adds that Dante places some pagans in paradise and another student begins to ask whether this counts as suicide.

speaker_notes.note: The final student intervention is cut off mid-question, but it clearly reopens the suicide problem by asking whether offering oneself should count as self-killing.

claims.claim: Jiang agrees that Jephthah's daughter is the hero of the biblical story because she willingly sacrifices herself so her father can keep the vow, and he says that nobility elevates her to paradise.

Jiang says this produces a Divine Comedy paradox: the formal rule is that a non-Christian cannot enter paradise, yet the intuitive nobility of the daughter's sacrifice seems to override that rule in her case.
In Jiang's retelling, the daughter's voluntary offering is what absolves the father of the direct guilt of killing her while still allowing the vow to be fulfilled.
Jiang clarifies that paradise is won not by a mere will to die but by a selfless act of love, with willing sacrifice serving only as the vehicle of that loving action.
Jiang uses the daughter to argue that there are pagans in paradise and that this is one of Divine Comedy's subversive pressures against the simple rule that only Christians are saved.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang names the daughter, not the father, as the hero of the story and then leaps past the formal rule to place her in paradise.
signature_moments.source_phrase: the daughter who is the hero of the story
signature_moments.why_it_matters: It reverses the entire frame of the Jephthah story, shifting attention from the father's rash vow to the daughter's noble self-offering.

signature_moments.moment: Jiang admits that the placement does not entirely make formal sense but insists that it makes intuitive sense.
signature_moments.source_phrase: it doesn't largely make sense but it makes intuitive sense
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This captures Jiang's willingness to privilege moral intuition and nobility over rigid rule-consistency when reading Dante's cosmos.

signature_moments.moment: The daughter's act is defined not as death-wish but as a selfless act of love that lifts her upward.
signature_moments.source_phrase: a selfless act of love is what elevates you to paradise
signature_moments.why_it_matters: This is the packet's most reusable doctrinal compression and becomes Jiang's criterion for salvation beyond mere identity or formal affiliation.

glossary_terms.definition_or_usage: Jiang's criterion for elevation to paradise: not mere desire or willingness, but an action grounded in sacrificial love for another.
Jiang's shorthand for the way Divine Comedy can place non-Christians in heaven when their acts embody a nobility or love that exceeds the formal salvation rule.

chronology_notes.note: This 2026-06-16 packet completes the daughter-side turn in the Jephthah discussion: after locating the father's failure in power, Jiang elevates the daughter through noble self-sacrifice and uses her case to press a broader claim that love can outrun Dante's formal Christian salvation boundary.

uncertainty_notes.note: Jiang's retelling treats the daughter's voluntary self-offering as easing or absolving the father's guilt, which is his interpretive frame in this seminar and not necessarily a neutral summary of every version of the biblical story.
The student's suicide objection is truncated, so only the direction of the question is certain.
